title: Shakuntala
hook: a king calls out at an empty hermitage, and the woman who answers sets terms before she says yes

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakuntala as a newborn by the river, guarded by birds and named for them by Kanva. Your line was Shakuntala. Did you thank someone who took care of you? Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

Who is here? That's the first thing King Dushyanta says at the hermitage. He has been hunting, he has left his soldiers behind, and he walks into the quiet place where the sage Kanva lives and calls out. Kanva isn't home. A young woman comes out instead, dressed like an ascetic, and welcomes him the way a host should. Then the king proposes marriage, almost at once, and the story waits to see what she'll say. What she says is not quite yes.
screen: `WHO IS HERE?` → `THE SAGE IS AWAY.` → `NOT QUITE YES.`

segments.voice: Start with the welcome. Shakuntala offers the king a seat and water and asks after his health, the duties of a host, and tells him her father has gone to gather fruit. Wait, she says, and he'll be back soon. The king asks who she is, and she tells him her birth, the sage, the apsara, the birds. Then he asks her to marry him. Her first answer is patience. Wait for my father, she says. He will give me to you. The king answers with law. He tells her there is a form of marriage called the gandharva, made by two people's own choice, and that it's lawful for a king. She can give herself. And here Shakuntala does the thing the rest of her story hangs on. She agrees, on one condition. Promise me, she says, that the son born of me will be your heir and rule after you. Only if you promise this. The king promises. They marry. He leaves for his city and says he will send for her, with a proper escort, to bring her to the palace. Then Kanva comes home. The epic says he knows what happened through his own inner sight, and he isn't angry. He's glad. He blesses her and tells her the marriage is a good one. Time goes by. She gives birth to a son, who grows up in the hermitage so strong that he tames the wild animals of the forest. The hermits call him the all-tamer. And from the city, nobody comes. Hold on to the condition she set. Shakuntala was young, alone, and asked by a king. She didn't just say yes. She asked for a promise, out loud. Tomorrow, that promise is the thing she carries into court.
screen: `SHE WELCOMES HIM AS A HOST` · `WAIT FOR MY FATHER` · `YES, IF YOU PROMISE ME THIS` · `THE BOY GROWS, AND NO ONE COMES`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it out loud. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind something you've agreed to lately, a plan, a job, a favor, a relationship. Ask yourself, gently: was there something I needed that I didn't say? Let one sentence form, simple and clear, the way Shakuntala said hers. You don't have to send it anywhere. Just hear it in your own voice, and breathe. If you pray, you can bring it into prayer. The bell holds the time.
Shakuntala. The young woman who welcomed a king, asked him to wait, and then said yes only on a promise spoken aloud. Today's word.
Your line: Shakuntala. Today, before you say yes to something, say the one thing you need from it. Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Hindus know this part of Shakuntala's story from the Mahabharata's first book, the Adi Parva, where the meeting and the gandharva marriage take place at Kanva's hermitage.

fork.setup: you're Shakuntala. a king you've just met says a marriage by your own choice is lawful, and asks you to marry him now. what do you say?
options: yes, if you promise my son will be your heir.
fork.reveal: she agrees on one condition, spoken aloud: her son will rule after him. the king promises, and later that promise goes to court.

original.note: Sanskrit: the gandharva form of marriage, made by the couple's own choice, which Dushyanta proposes to Shakuntala.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shakuntala was swept off her feet.
what it means: she welcomed him as a host, asked him to wait, and then set a condition before saying yes.
what a scholar hears: in the epic, her condition is that her son be heir, and the whole court scene later turns on that promise.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Dushyanta at Kanva's hermitage; Shakuntala's welcome; his proposal; the gandharva marriage; her condition that her son be heir; Kanva's return and blessing; the birth and boyhood of her son)

notes: Confirm the order: welcome, her birth told, proposal, 'wait for my father', the king's account of the gandharva form, her condition (her son to be heir apparent), his promise, his promise to send an escort. The epic numbers the forms of marriage; the count was left out.
Confirm Kanva knows by inner (spiritual) sight and approves. The boon she asks of him was left out.
'The all-tamer': the boy's name Sarvadamana as the hermits give it; the Sanskrit name was left out of the voice so as not to step on day 1352, which names him Bharata.
The epic says the boy grows for some years in the hermitage before Kanva sends them to court; the span was left out under the claims rule.
Editor pass: 'the thing that turns the whole story' toned down; otherwise unchanged.
